title: Completing or Refusing Low-Dimensional Records of Structured Quantum Circuits: Measurement Loss, Compression Loss, and Hardware Drift
abstract: Structured quantum circuits are often summarized by low-dimensional records. Records lose control-dependent information when they merge outcomes whose probabilities respond differently to circuit parameters. We assess this loss without a parametric hardware-noise model or low-dimensional statistical family. Quantum Fisher information bounds premeasurement sensitivity; Fisher metrics of measurements and records describe device-attainable sensitivity. A Hellinger residual measures the response removed by a record, while its local quadratic term is the conditional covariance of the full-outcome score. Simultaneous confidence bounds support approval, refusal, or deferral.   We prove a finite-library completion theorem: executable augmentations terminate with either a record preserving every declared response or proof that no library augmentation removes the loss. For an analytic control germ, integral closures characterize preservation along every analytic control arc, and finitely many Rees valuations detect failure. This state--measurement--record chain connects an all-arc criterion to executable completion or refusal, an attainable-Fisher local kernel criterion, and finite-sample decisions.   A three-qubit calculation separates measurement loss from record loss. IBM experiments on Kingston and Marrakesh test decisions in fixed-particle-number and GHZ families, including negative controls. An end-to-end Kingston experiment reduces calibration shots by 33.3% while meeting prespecified noninferiority criteria on two held-out objectives. In two-epoch IQM Garnet data, median record-level drift is 0.0797 times full-distribution drift, but a significant residual remains in 35 of 36 settings. These experiments validate failure detection on the tested circuits; they do not establish universal compression performance or device quantum Fisher information.
summary: This work develops a comprehensive framework to audit low-dimensional records summarizing quantum circuits, quantifying information loss due to measurement or compression. It merges quantum information theory with algebraic geometry to create an executable 'approve/refuse/defer' decision protocol. This is vital for building reliable quantum hardware by certifying that simplified measurements retain sufficient fidelity to the true quantum process.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental challenge of determining if a low-dimensional statistical record of a structured quantum circuit accurately preserves the full quantum information, accounting for measurement loss, compression loss, and hardware drift.
main_result: The authors establish a rigorous, executable 'completion-or-refusal' procedure based on algebraic criteria, allowing for finite-sample decisions (Approve, Refuse, or Defer) regarding the fidelity of the low-dimensional record.
method: The methodology combines advanced quantum information metrics (Quantum Fisher Information, Hellinger residual) with tools from algebraic geometry (integral closures, Rees valuations) to create a multi-stage audit framework.
model_or_system: The system involves structured quantum circuits implemented on quantum hardware, whose outcomes are summarized by low-dimensional records. The analysis models the process through stages: initial state, circuit evolution, measurement, and final record compression.
key_observables: Hellinger residual, simultaneous confidence bounds, quantum Fisher information metrics ($g_{SLD}, g_{Q,e}, g_{T,e,a}$), and the decision outcomes: Approve, Refuse, Defer.
important_parameters: Circuit parameters ($	heta$), noise models (avoided assumption), finite-sample size, and the declared loss budget.
main_assumptions: The method aims to avoid assuming a specific parametric hardware-noise model or a low-dimensional statistical family, though the final experimental validation is limited to specific backends and circuits.
figures_summary: Figure 1 summarizes two analysis routes: a default finite-data audit and an optional algebraic audit using response ideals, explicitly separating the two decision paths.
paper_structure: The paper develops a theoretical framework connecting all-arc criteria (algebraic/global) to executable, finite-sample decision procedures (local/experimental), culminating in hardware tests on specific circuit families.
why_interesting: It provides a mathematically rigorous, general framework for quantifying and certifying the information loss when abstracting complex quantum processes into simplified, hardware-friendly metrics, which is crucial for scaling quantum computation.
